name: Saint Barthélemy
summary_text: Saint Barthélemy stands under the national framework of France. Criminal law, rules on identity documents, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in metropolitan France.  Same-sex sexual activity is not criminalised. Private same-sex relations were removed from criminal liability by the Penal Code of 1791 and remained absent from the Penal Code of 1810 as applied in French colonies. The unequal age of consent introduced in 1942 was equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982.  Since 1 January 2017, under the law signed on 18 November 2016, a transgender person can obtain legal change of gender without sex reassignment surgery, sterilisation, psychiatric certificates or medical diagnosis. The application must go before a court. Change of first name can be made separately at the registry office. Non-binary identity is not recognised in French law, so a visitor whose documents record a non-binary marker has no legal counterpart on arrival.  Discrimination on the basis of sexual identity was prohibited in July 2012. The term was replaced by gender identity in Penal Code article 225-1 and in the Labour Code by the law of 18 November 2016. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation in employment, housing and access to goods and services was prohibited in 1985. The law of 31 December 2004 made homophobic comments punishable by a maximum of 45,000 euro fine and 12 months imprisonment and increased penalties where physical assault or murder was motivated by the sexual orientation of the victim. Since 2017 transphobia constitutes an aggravating circumstance for all crimes punishable by prison.  Same-sex marriage is legal in Saint Barthélemy. It was approved by the National Assembly on 12 February 2013 and the Senate on 12 April 2013, ruled constitutional on 17 May 2013 and signed on 18 May 2013, with the first ceremony held on 29 May 2013. Joint adoption by same-sex couples has been legal since May 2013.  Conversion practices are prohibited. The Senate voted on 7 December 2020, the National Assembly concurred on 25 January 2022 and the ban was published on 1 February 2022. The stated penalty is two years imprisonment and a 30,000 euro fine.  Gender-affirming hormone therapy and surgery are covered by the French framework. One source dates availability to 1975 and another dates domestic legalisation of surgery to 1979. In 2010 France removed gender identity disorder as a diagnosis by decree. Access on the island itself is reported as limited. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report recorded lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable geographic access for gender-affirming healthcare in France. A visitor requiring such care should expect to rely on provision outside Saint Barthélemy.  Detention falls under the French system. Reporting on that system by the controller-general of detention places finds that trans detainees, overwhelmingly women held under birth-sex placement, suffer the most in prison and that administration policy recognises only biological sex. A 2011 case in Nantes resulted in placement of a trans woman in a men’s prison. The opinion of 25 May 2021 on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, based on about 40 referrals since 2010, found that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention. Its recommendations were stated to apply also to intersex and non-binary persons.  The social environment described for visitors is open and accepting. The luxury-yacht economy has long welcomed gay couples. Same-sex couples are reported to attract no attention and no hostility is noted. Discretion is described as the norm among a high-end visitor population. There are no LGBTQ venues or visible scene and no Pride-specific events. Hotel staff are described as trained for diverse guests.
